name: Raw vegan diet
lead: A raw vegan diet consists of uncooked plant foods, typically fruit, vegetables, nuts, seeds and sprouts, usually kept below roughly 40-49 degrees Celsius. It excludes animal products and, in many versions, most cooked or processed foods.[8] It is discussed in appearance communities as a route to better skin, leanness and general health.

Studies are small and mostly observational. A study of long-term followers of a mostly raw vegan diet reported vitamin B12 status concerns, a cross-sectional study linked a low-calorie raw vegan diet and endurance exercise with low cardiometabolic risk factors, and case reports describe both athletic performance and complications.[1][2][4][7] No trial has tested the diet for skin or facial appearance.
Dietetic sources note that cooking does not simply destroy nutrients, and that raw vegan diets may be low in vitamin B12, vitamin D and calories.[8]
infobox: Raw fruit, vegetables, nuts, seeds, sprouts

paras: Raw foodism has a long history. The Wikipedia article cites early ascetic examples, a Swiss sanatorium opened in 1904 serving raw food, an American raw food restaurant in 1917, and popularisation by authors in the 1970s and 1980s.[8]

Proponents hold that heating food above about 40-48 degrees destroys enzymes and nutrients and that raw eating prevents disease. The Wikipedia article describes these claims as not supported by nutrition science, noting that food enzymes are digested rather than playing a major role in digestion and that cooking can raise availability of some nutrients.[8]

In a study of long-term followers of the Hallelujah diet, a mostly raw vegan pattern, researchers measured B12 markers and followed participants given different supplement forms.[1] A cross-sectional study of sedentary people on a low-calorie, low-protein raw vegan diet reported lower cardiometabolic risk factors than comparison groups.[2]

A pilot study of guests at a raw vegan institute reported changes in quality of life and immune markers over a one- to three-week stay.[3] Research on adherence suggests the diet is hard to maintain.[6] A study of dental parameters examined periodontal and dental effects.[5] A case report described an ultra-triathlete eating raw vegan, and a paediatric case report described small bowel obstruction in a child on a strict raw vegan diet.[4][7]

Human research is limited to small observational studies, pilot studies and case reports on nutrition, cardiometabolic markers, adherence, dental health and athletic performance.[1][2][3][4][5][6][7] No studies were found on skin, face or looks outcomes.

timeline.event: A Swiss sanatorium serving raw food opens.[8]
An early American raw food restaurant opens.[8]
Study of B12 status in long-term mostly raw vegan dieters published.[1]

lore.intro: Raw veganism appears in forum threads about diet and health, sometimes alongside meat-based and fruit-heavy alternatives.[L1]

claims.claim: Raw vegan eating improves skin and overall health.
claims.believers: Followers say uncooked plants retain enzymes and nutrients and produce clearer skin and energy.
claims.experts: No trial tests skin outcomes. Dietetic sources say enzyme claims are not supported and note possible B12 and vitamin D shortfalls.[8][1]

claims.claim: Raw diets are risky for children.
claims.believers: Some forum users argue instead for animal-based diets with fruit.[9]
claims.experts: A case report describes bowel obstruction in a child on a strict raw vegan diet, and a 2004 review flagged developmental concerns.[7][8]

card.summary: Uncooked plant-only eating: small studies on nutrition, none on looks, and B12 is a recurring concern.
card.note: B12 and vitamin D shortfalls reported; child cases documented.

quick.overview:
A raw vegan diet is made of uncooked plant foods kept below roughly 40-49 degrees Celsius. People in appearance communities explore it for skin and leanness.

Research is limited to small observational studies and case reports; none examined appearance.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say heat destroys enzymes and nutrients. Dietetic sources say food enzymes are digested rather than doing digestive work and that cooking can improve availability of some nutrients.
quick.risks: Reported concerns include low B12, vitamin D and calories, and case reports of problems in children.
